# Comprehensive and Accurate Cislunar Situational Awareness: An Operational Guide for Short-Term Tracking and Monitoring

Comprehensive cislunar situational awareness requires a networked, layered system rather than a single sensor or catalog. The system must search for known and unknown objects, detect and recognize them, maintain custody, estimate their states with defensible uncertainty, identify maneuvers and behavior changes, predict future trajectories with Earth–Moon–Sun dynamics, and deliver alerts quickly enough to support mission decisions. The most effective architecture combines optical, infrared, radar, passive-radio-frequency, Deep Space Network, telemetry, onboard-navigation, and crosslink measurements with adaptive tasking and a high-fidelity, uncertainty-aware catalog.

The evidence also establishes important limits. Cislunar space has no universally adopted boundary, populated passive catalog, common completeness baseline, mission-agnostic short-term horizon, or common latency and acceptance thresholds. Existing demonstrations—such as CAPSTONE, Artemis I, DSN navigation, lunar and cislunar sensor studies, and emerging TraCSS services—validate important components, but not yet a comprehensive, independently validated cislunar awareness system.

## Roadmap

The report first defines the operational contract: what “comprehensive,” “accurate,” “timely,” and “short-term” should mean, and which objects must be covered. It then explains the dynamics and observing conditions that determine whether a target can be detected, localized, identified, and predicted.

The central sections compare sensor phenomenologies, observer locations, estimation methods, catalogs, and tasking policies. They then describe a closed operational loop from observation through alerting, followed by measurable effectiveness criteria and validation scenarios. The final sections connect the guidance to CAPSTONE, Artemis I, Orion, the DSN, SPICE, current exchange standards, and the remaining interoperability and resilience constraints.

## 1. Define the operational contract before building the system

### Cislunar space needs an explicit boundary convention

“Cislunar space” is not a single universally accepted geometric volume. The United States has been described as using a boundary extending from Earth to the region around the lunar surface, while other definitions emphasize the region from GEO outward, the Earth–Moon gravitationally influenced volume, or an approximate altitude of 550,000 km. The AFRL primer defines it more physically as the volume influenced by Earth and/or the Moon, and discusses a region extending to 12 GEO, just beyond the Earth–Moon L2 region. A proposed cislunar tracking-message architecture extends its intended applicability to trajectories up to 2 million km from Earth and to cislunar and Earth–Sun Lagrange regions. ([Space ISAC incident-response framework](https://spaceisac.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/2025.03.04-Cislunar-Incident-Response-1.pdf); [AFRL cislunar primer](https://www.afrl.af.mil/Portals/90/Documents/RV/A%20Primer%20on%20Cislunar%20Space_Dist%20A_PA2021-1271.pdf?ver=vs6e0sE4PuJ51QC-15DEfg%3D%3D); [proposed cislunar SSA message set](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/cislunar_ssa_proposed_message_set-nov2021_rev2_without_emailspdf.pdf))

A practical operational system should therefore use a boundary made of volumes and corridors rather than a single radial cutoff:

- The core region should extend from Earth through the Earth–Moon transit volume to the lunar vicinity and surface.
- The catalog should explicitly include Earth–Moon L1–L5, nearby Lyapunov, halo, Lissajous, butterfly, distant prograde, and distant retrograde orbits.
- Translunar departure and return corridors should be included whenever they intersect the operational volume.
- An extended region should cover objects that can enter, leave, or transit through the core region during the prediction horizon.
- Every observation, track, and catalog release should carry a boundary or region label, such as Earth–Moon transit, lunar orbit, NRHO, L1/L2 region, or extended cislunar transfer.

This is an operational convention, not an adopted international standard. The important requirement is that the boundary be stated before completeness or coverage is measured. A system cannot claim “complete cislunar awareness” if its denominator changes between a GEO-to-Moon volume, a 550,000-km sphere, and a two-million-kilometer transfer region.

### The target population must include more than active spacecraft

The target population should be organized by both physical object class and operational status.

| Target class | Objects to include | Required operational information |
|---|---|---|
| Cooperative spacecraft | Crewed vehicles, robotic spacecraft, relay satellites, lunar orbiters, Gateway, navigation and communications platforms | Identity, mission status, operator, planned ephemeris, telemetry, maneuver plan, covariance |
| Non-cooperative spacecraft | Unknown or unresponsive spacecraft, foreign or commercial spacecraft without shared data, maneuvering vehicles | State, uncertainty, behavioral indicators, RF and optical signatures, association hypotheses |
| Launch hardware | Launch vehicles, upper stages, injection stages, adapters, deployment mechanisms | Parent launch, separation events, expected trajectory, fragment or payload associations |
| Debris and inactive objects | Released hardware, fragmentation products, abandoned spacecraft, operational debris | Object type, size or signature estimate, state, covariance, origin hypothesis, collision relevance |
| Unknown and natural objects | Unresolved detections, possible asteroids or other transient bodies entering the operational volume | Discovery tracklet, admissible region, classification confidence, follow-up priority |

The catalog should not silently exclude an object because it is inactive, non-cooperative, RF-silent, or absent from an operator’s ephemeris. NASA’s 2023 cislunar-demand analysis distinguishes persistent custody of existing assets from monitoring translunar transfers and newly deployed segments. It specifically identifies deployed daughter spacecraft and returning or outbound transfer vehicles as additional objects requiring monitoring. ([Tomita, Shimane, and Ho](https://doi.org/10.64861/gbke2290))

A natural object does not need to be cataloged in the same way as a spacecraft, but it should enter the operational target set when it can create a conjunction, interfere with a mission, or explain a detection. The 2026 Earth–Moon tracking study, for example, includes an Apophis close-approach arc as a non-cooperative target case alongside lunar-orbit and L4 cases. ([Optical astrometry and radar ranging study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1134/S0038094626600563))

### Awareness is a chain of products, not a single label

A useful cislunar awareness system should produce a progressive set of products:

1. A search record indicating where and when the sensor searched, with detection sensitivity and non-detection information.
2. A detection record containing time-tagged measurements, measurement covariance, sensor calibration state, and a provisional association.
3. A tracklet containing consecutive observations, a provisional trajectory or admissible region, and competing association hypotheses.
4. A recognized-object record containing object type, identity candidates, signature information, and confidence.
5. A custody track containing a state estimate, covariance or ensemble, dynamic model, maneuver history, observation provenance, and next recommended observation.
6. A prediction product containing future state distributions, event times, visibility windows, conjunction candidates, and expected uncertainty.
7. A mission-status or alert product describing whether the object is active, maneuvering, lost, degraded, or potentially hazardous.

The 2025 CSSA capability decomposition uses four related functions—search, detection, recognition, and tracking. Search locates objects in a volume; detection distinguishes an object from background; recognition classifies its type; and tracking maintains its trajectory and predicts future positions. ([DeCoster et al., “Building the Future of Cislunar Surveillance”](https://doi.org/10.1177/21680256251390412))

The operational distinction matters. A detected point is not necessarily an identified spacecraft. A good orbit estimate is not necessarily a reliable mission-status assessment. A catalog record without a covariance is not sufficient for short-term conjunction assessment.

### Define completeness, accuracy, timeliness, and confidence separately

A defensible definition of comprehensive awareness is conditional:

> The system is comprehensive over a declared target population, region, time interval, sensor availability state, and detection threshold when it detects, associates, and maintains usable products for the required fraction of truth objects and observation opportunities.

This definition avoids equating “comprehensive” with impossible continuous visibility of every object. It also forces reporting of the denominator. Completeness should be measured separately for cooperative spacecraft, non-cooperative objects, debris, unknowns, and target sizes or signatures.

Accuracy should include at least:

- position error at the observation epoch;
- velocity error;
- predicted position and velocity error at specified lead times;
- covariance consistency;
- uncertainty growth during observation gaps;
- maneuver-estimation error;
- identity or recognition error;
- event-time error for occultations, perilune passages, conjunctions, or expected contacts.

Timeliness should be measured from the physical event to a usable operational product, not merely from sensor exposure to a stored file. Useful timestamps include:

- observation time to local detection;
- observation time to track initiation;
- measurement receipt to fused state;
- maneuver indication to reprocessed state;
- state update to alert publication;
- alert publication to operator acknowledgment;
- task assignment to sensor execution.

Confidence should not be reduced to covariance size. A small covariance with an incorrect object association is dangerous. Confidence should combine state consistency, association probability, identity evidence, sensor provenance, dynamic-model adequacy, and the age of the latest supporting observation.

No common cislunar baseline for these quantities was established in the supplied evidence. They must therefore be specified in each mission or network concept of operations and reported with the sensor class, target class, geometry, and prediction horizon.

### Operationalize “short term” without pretending there is a universal cutoff

No mission-agnostic short-term horizon or common task-completion cutoff has been established. The most defensible approach is to define the horizon relative to the decision being supported.

| Horizon | Typical purpose | Product |
|---|---|---|
| Immediate: seconds to minutes | Confirm a detection, resolve an association, protect a sensor handoff, detect an abrupt maneuver | Measurement-quality record, track update, immediate cue |
| Short operational: minutes to hours | Maintain custody through a pass, fill an observation gap, process a maneuver, issue an alert | Updated state and covariance, next-pass task, alert |
| Event horizon: several observations to one orbit | Predict a perilune, occultation, conjunction, or relay opportunity | Event-centered ephemeris and observation plan |
| NRHO-scale horizon: about one revolution | Monitor a Gateway-like orbit over its approximately 6.5-day revolution | Full-period uncertainty and coverage assessment |
| Extended tactical horizon: days to weeks | Plan station keeping, transfer-corridor surveillance, or long-gap recovery | Ensemble prediction and contingency tasking |

A six-and-a-half-day one-revolution horizon is a concrete analytical proxy for a 9:2 NRHO, not a universal short-term standard. A 2026 uncertainty study found that position and velocity disagreement between two propagation formulations increased by approximately an order of magnitude near the perilune crossing about 3.25 days into a roughly 6.5-day revolution. ([Cislunar state and uncertainty propagation](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.20110v1))

For a particular task, the short-term horizon should end when one of three conditions occurs: the decision deadline passes, the next required event is completed, or uncertainty exceeds the task’s allowable bound. This is more meaningful than declaring every prediction shorter than an arbitrary number of days to be “short term.”

## 2. Model the dynamics and observing conditions together

### Earth–Moon–Sun dynamics determine the prediction problem

Cislunar motion cannot generally be represented as a two-body Keplerian orbit. Earth and Moon gravity are both dynamically important, solar gravity affects both trajectory and illumination, and solar-radiation pressure can become a leading model error for small or high-area-to-mass-ratio spacecraft.

The circular restricted three-body problem (CR3BP) is useful for understanding Earth–Moon orbit families, Lagrange-point geometry, periodic trajectories, and first-order observability. The bicircular restricted four-body problem (BCR4BP) adds time-varying solar geometry and is useful for illumination and Sun–Earth–Moon visibility studies. Neither should be treated as the final operational model for a precision catalog.

An operational propagator should normally include:

- Earth and Moon point-mass and nonspherical gravity;
- solar and relevant planetary third-body gravity;
- a current planetary and lunar ephemeris;
- relativistic and tidal terms when required by the accuracy budget;
- solar radiation pressure;
- spacecraft area-to-mass ratio and attitude information when available;
- thrust, station keeping, deployment, and maneuver hypotheses;
- reference-frame and time-scale transformations;
- stochastic process noise or a calibrated model-discrepancy representation.

The 2026 high-fidelity propagation study uses JPL DE440 ephemerides for its Earth–Moon–Sun model and propagates 10,000-member Monte Carlo ensembles to examine nonlinear uncertainty growth. ([Cislunar state and uncertainty propagation](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.20110v1)) The 2021 optical-observability study, by contrast, uses CR3BP for orbit-family comparisons and an empirical observability Gramian. These are complementary uses of model fidelity, not competing claims that one model is universally sufficient.

### Different orbit regimes create different awareness problems

| Regime | Dynamic and geometric character | Main awareness problem | Operational consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Translunar and return trajectories | High-energy or low-energy transfers, often with changing Earth and lunar influence | Long arcs, changing range, weak apparent motion, and uncertain arrival or departure timing | Monitor corridors and event windows rather than relying on uniform global revisit |
| Low lunar orbit | Strong lunar gravity-field effects, short periods, lunar occultation, and limited surface visibility | Fast state evolution and frequent Moon blockage | Use lunar or cislunar observers, high-fidelity lunar gravity, and short revisit intervals |
| NRHO | Highly eccentric, three-body orbit with long apolune residence and rapid perilune passage | Geometry and relative velocity change sharply within one revolution | Schedule phase-dependent observations and treat perilune as a high-sensitivity interval |
| Halo and Lyapunov orbits | Periodic or quasi-periodic motion near collinear Lagrange points, often unstable or station-keeping dependent | Target-dependent observability and loss of custody after gaps | Select observer orbits for geometric diversity, not merely proximity |
| Lagrange regions and nearby LPOs | L1–L3 are unstable saddle regions; L4 and L5 have locally stable volumes; nearby families vary in period and amplitude | Small errors or maneuvers can move an object away from a nominal family | Maintain families of hypotheses and use model-aware association |
| DRO, DPO, and other lunar-centered periodic orbits | Relatively persistent geometric structures but with lunar occultation and solar perturbation | Earth-based range and angular diversity can be weak | Combine lunar, space-based, optical, RF, and range measurements |

The AFRL primer notes that L1, L2, L3, most repeating natural trajectories, and quasi-periodic orbits are unstable. Once custody is lost, even a non-maneuvering object can depart substantially from its nominal repeating orbit. Small volumes around L4 and L5 are exceptions with greater long-duration stability. ([AFRL cislunar primer](https://www.afrl.af.mil/Portals/90/Documents/RV/A%20Primer%20on%20Cislunar%20Space_Dist%20A_PA2021-1271.pdf?ver=vs6e0sE4PuJ51QC-15DEfg%3D%3D))

CAPSTONE demonstrates the operational meaning of this geometry. NASA describes its NRHO as bringing the spacecraft within about 1,000 miles of one lunar pole and about 43,500 miles from the other at its peak, approximately every seven days, while retaining an unobstructed Earth view and lunar South Pole coverage. ([NASA CAPSTONE mission page](https://www.nasa.gov/smallspacecraft/capstone/))

### Visibility is not the same as observability

Visibility asks whether a target can be seen at all. Observability asks how much the available measurements reveal about the target state.

A target can be visible but poorly observable if it produces nearly constant line-of-sight angles, has insufficient range diversity, or is observed from a geometry that makes position and velocity errors nearly indistinguishable. Conversely, a target can be visible for a shorter interval but highly observable if the line of sight changes in a way that separates state components.

Fowler, Hurtt, and Paley quantify this distinction with an empirical local observability Gramian. Its condition number compares the largest and smallest singular values; a large condition number indicates an ill-conditioned estimation problem, while a smaller value indicates better local observability. Their simulation used a line-of-sight unit vector and range measurement in a CR3BP environment, so its numerical percentages are geometry-study results rather than universal sensor performance. ([Fowler, Hurtt, and Paley](https://cdcl.umd.edu/papers/jass.pdf))

The study found that L2 halo targets were 37–65% more observable from lunar and Lagrange-point observers than from Earth observers, and L1 Lyapunov targets were 10–71% more observable. In other pairings, L2 Lyapunov targets were 56–200% less observable from those non-Earth observers, and L1 halo targets were generally as much as 141% less observable, although particular L1 observer pairings improved L1 halo observability by up to 20%. These results demonstrate target dependence, not a universal ranking of observer orbits.

The practical conclusion is that observer selection must be evaluated against the target family and measurement type. There is no single optimal cislunar observer orbit. Fowler and Paley therefore propose a heterogeneous network involving Earth, L2 halo, L4, and L1 Lyapunov observers. Their two-observer analysis concatenates each observer’s line-of-sight and range measurements and can be extended beyond two observers. ([Fowler and Paley](https://cdcl.umd.edu/papers/jass.pdf))

### Occultation, eclipse, exclusion angles, and illumination create structured gaps

A cislunar system must predict both positive and negative observation opportunities. Important causes of missed observations include:

- Earth or Moon occultation;
- lunar-surface horizon limits;
- eclipse and shadow;
- Sun and Moon exclusion angles;
- daylight and local atmospheric conditions for ground sensors;
- sensor field-of-view limits;
- target phase angle and reflected-light loss;
- thermal state and infrared background;
- RF link geometry and emitter antenna orientation;
- observer power, pointing, and communications availability.

Ground optical observations are especially sensitive to phase angle and background. A 2021 cislunar optical study found that its simulated selected DRO remained only partly observable with a limiting magnitude of 16, with lunar background interference around 200–300 hours and additional gaps after approximately 650 hours. The study did not include local weather, so its coverage is an optimistic geometry and radiometry result. ([Cislunar SSA, AAS 21-290](https://engineering.purdue.edu/people/kathleen.howell.1/Publications/Conferences/2021_AAS_FruHowDeMBha.pdf))

A separate photometry study found that cislunar objects are unresolved at typical ground or space-based viewing distances and that objects near the Moon or L1/L2 can repeat photometric behavior on a lunar-cycle timescale. In a simulated Chandrayaan-2 case, the target was completely unobservable from the Starfire Optical Range during selected lunar-orbit segments because it was too close to the Moon, while a Moon-based observer had its own horizon gaps. ([Dao et al.](https://amostech.com/TechnicalPapers/2020/Cislunar-SSA/Dao.pdf))

BCR4BP-based visibility work reaches the same operational conclusion: Sun and Moon motion must be modeled together. In one illustrative month-long simulation with assumed exclusion angles of 50° for the Sun, 30° for Earth, and 35° for the Moon, no location achieved 100% visibility from all observers. The result used simplified target and detection assumptions, so it should be used to design stress cases, not as a universal coverage number. ([Bhadauria and Frueh](https://amostech.com/TechnicalPapers/2022/Cislunar-SSA/Bhadauria.pdf))

### Prediction uncertainty can become non-Gaussian and target-dependent

For a nonlinear state model, a covariance ellipse is only a local approximation. During a long gap, uncertainty can stretch, bend, split, or develop multiple modes. A cislunar prediction should therefore use one or more of:

- sigma-point propagation;
- Gaussian-mixture propagation;
- particle or Monte Carlo ensembles;
- unscented or higher-order transforms;
- differential correction and collocation;
- interval or admissible-region methods;
- model-error ensembles for alternate maneuver and SRP hypotheses.

A 2021 Monte Carlo study propagated 1,000 samples for 30 days using both simplified and full-ephemeris models. The full model produced asymmetric, curved, clustered, crossing, and coil-like uncertainty distributions, with transfer-orbit asymmetry visible by 10 days. The study’s initial 10-m position and 10-m/s velocity dispersions were assumptions for that experiment, not generic cislunar uncertainty values. ([Cislunar SSA, AAS 21-290](https://engineering.purdue.edu/people/kathleen.howell.1/Publications/Conferences/2021_AAS_FruHowDeMBha.pdf))

Solar radiation pressure is an especially important model-error source for distant cislunar orbits. A 2026 study identifies it as the third-largest perturbation after lunisolar gravity for DRO, NRHO, and triangular-libration-point satellites and as a primary factor limiting orbit-determination accuracy. It also reports that no commonly adopted empirical cislunar SRP model yet exists. Analytical and semi-analytical models need spacecraft attitude, which may be unavailable for non-cooperative targets. ([A new SRP model for cislunar orbits](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.01775))

The proposed Empirical NJU Cislunar Model improved simulated orbit-determination results relative to cannonball and ECOM models in several scenario-specific tests. For example, in one simulated DRO case with Earth-fixed attitude, the reported RMS position error was 16.48 m with the ENCM, compared with 20,655 m for the cannonball model and 5,144.69 m for ECOM. Other cases, including NRHO, produced different error levels, and the tests used a simulated box-wing truth model with no random measurement noise. The result supports model development, but it is not an operational accuracy guarantee.

## 3. Build a layered sensing and communications architecture

### No single phenomenology covers the target population

The sensor architecture should be designed by function rather than by a search for one universally superior sensor.

| Measurement layer | Typical measurements | Strengths | Main limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Visible optical | Angles, streaks, photometry, resolved imagery | Large fields of view, passive operation, useful shape and brightness information, strong angular measurements | Illumination, phase angle, background, weather, exclusion angles, and no direct range from a single unresolved image |
| Thermal infrared | Angles, thermal brightness, imagery | More stable visibility across illumination conditions; can detect warm targets invisible in VIS | Lower spatial resolution at equal aperture and range; depends on target temperature and thermal model |
| Active radar | Range, range-rate, angle, Doppler, radar cross section | Direct metric information; can work without reflected sunlight; useful for precision tracking and maneuver detection | Power, aperture, beam dwell, RCS fluctuation, two-way path loss, clutter and sidelobes |
| Passive RF | TDOA, FDOA, emitter timing, modulation, RF signature | Day/night and weather-independent; high cadence; can characterize emitters and sometimes identify spacecraft | Requires an emitting target, synchronized stations, suitable baselines, signal access, and association across stations |
| Cooperative radiometric navigation | DSN range, range-rate, Doppler, Delta-DOR, telemetry | High-quality state and clock information for cooperative spacecraft; supports mission navigation | Scheduling, Earth-centered geometry, operator cooperation, and weak applicability to silent or deceptive objects |
| Onboard and crosslink navigation | Optical navigation, inter-spacecraft range and range-rate, telemetry and health data | Reduces dependence on Earth; can provide frequent local updates and mission-status information | Requires participating spacecraft, calibrated time and frames, and cannot reveal non-cooperative objects |

### Optical sensing is the broad search and characterization layer

Small optical sensors can provide wide fields of view and rapid search, especially when distributed across multiple cislunar observer orbits. In the DeCoster et al. architecture study, a modeled 10-cm optical sensor could scan a full 4π steradian volume in roughly 10 hours under its assumed conditions, while a 10-m sensor took roughly 100 days because of its smaller field of view. A modeled network of 18.5-cm sensors provided up to 65% detection coverage over the study’s 30-day, two-dimensional domain. Those values assumed a representative large object, favorable optical modeling, and specific orbit architectures. They should not be interpreted as generic performance for faint debris. ([DeCoster et al.](https://doi.org/10.1177/21680256251390412))

Optical detections normally begin as angles-only measurements. They are valuable for search, photometric characterization, and cueing another sensor, but a single unresolved optical sensor does not directly determine range. DeCoster et al. explicitly note that their small-optical architecture supplied angle information but no range, making it only partially sufficient for queuing follow-up sensors.

Large optical apertures can support recognition when a target is resolved. In the same study, visible sensors were modeled as having roughly ten times better resolution than 10-μm long-wave infrared at the same range and aperture, although infrared had a potential signal-to-noise advantage for warm targets. The model required very large effective apertures for meaningful resolved recognition over the modeled domain, and its 1,000-m end members were a performance envelope motivated by in-space assembly rather than a near-term hardware claim.

A practical optical layer should therefore combine:

- wide-field search sensors;
- narrow-field precision astrometry;
- photometric and light-curve processing;
- visible and infrared channels where target temperature and illumination justify them;
- track-before-detect processing for faint, slowly moving objects;
- resolved or partially resolved imagery for recognition when geometry permits.

The University of Maryland’s FaXT project illustrates the value of track-before-detect processing. FaXT had detected asteroid objects up to ten times fainter than previously possible in its original application, and the project proposes adapting it to cislunar targets such as CAPSTONE. The ten-times-fainter result belongs to asteroid searches; it is not a measured cislunar performance result. ([University of Maryland FaXT project](https://tamz.umd.edu/project/rapid_disco/))

### Infrared is a complement to visible optical sensing

A 2026 numerical comparison of visible and thermal-infrared sensors modeled Lyapunov and halo targets viewed by four space-based observers. Visible sensors produced higher position accuracy under favorable illumination but lost observability when Sun–target–observer geometry reduced signal-to-noise ratio. Thermal infrared produced lower spatial accuracy but more stable signal-to-noise behavior and visibility for targets not detectable in the visible band. Weighted least-squares triangulation of VIS and IR measurements increased observation opportunities and improved IR-only estimates while retaining the high accuracy of VIS-only cases. ([Takahashi and Barnhart](https://arc.aiaa.org/doi/10.2514/6.2026-3092))

The operational implication is not that infrared replaces visible optical sensing. It is a gap-filling layer for illumination-driven outages, particularly when the target is warm and recognition is not the immediate objective.

### Active radar supplies metric measurements but does not solve the coverage problem alone

Active radar can provide direct range, range-rate, Doppler, and angular measurements, making it attractive for precision tracking and maneuver detection. Its limits are the radar equation, transmit power, aperture, beamwidth, dwell time, RCS fluctuation, and the fourth-power dependence of received power on range in monostatic operation.

A 2025 modeled architecture used an active-RF detection target with a 7,854 m² radar cross section and a 10-m cylindrical body. Under its coherent-detection assumptions, it selected a 95% probability of detection, a 10⁻⁴ false-alarm probability, and an 11.6-dB signal-to-noise requirement. The study’s eight-aperture platform could search for that large modeled object in approximately 5.5 hours at 100,000 km, whereas a 1-m² target required much longer modeled scan times. ([DeCoster et al.](https://doi.org/10.1177/21680256251390412))

For a modeled 100-m active-RF sensor at 100,000 km, the same study reports range accuracy on the order of hundreds of meters, velocity accuracy on the order of 100 m/s, and angular accuracy on the order of 0.15 mrad at the stated signal-to-noise ratio. Its conclusion of 100% custody assumed continuous monitoring. That assumption is precisely what a real network must test rather than presume.

Active radar is therefore most valuable in a tiered system:

- wide-area search or corridor monitoring for sufficiently large RCS;
- precision follow-up after an optical or passive-RF cue;
- range and range-rate updates that collapse angles-only uncertainty;
- high-cadence observation during maneuvers or close approaches;
- local sensing around a cislunar asset.

The 2026 CisLunarSense study illustrates a different radar concept: opportunistic sensing using a Gateway Ka-band communication relay. Its CR3BP-based, author-selected model predicts detection of operational debris below 50 m/s within 700 km and more than 30 minutes of warning, with external threats up to 500 m/s detectable within 400–630 km. Orbit-phase-adaptive allocation reduces modeled sensing duty cycle from 60% to 19% while increasing relay throughput from 44 to 90 Mbps. The analysis assumes future multicarrier relay capability even though the current HLCS baseline is single-carrier, so these are promising design results rather than operational measurements. ([CisLunarSense](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.10807v1))

### Passive RF fills optical gaps and characterizes emitters

Passive RF systems can provide TDOA and FDOA measurements, exploit target transmissions, and operate during darkness or unfavorable optical weather. Their limitations are equally important: an RF-silent object may be invisible, target antenna orientation matters, baselines must be synchronized, and several stations must observe compatible signals.

The WeTrack passive-RF architecture synchronizes stations with GPS and Galileo, sends signal snapshots to a processing center, and estimates TDOA and FDOA with cross-ambiguity processing. Its stated normal cadence is about 40 minutes and its intense cadence about five minutes; it advertises day/night and weather-independent collection, maneuver characterization, RF-behavior characterization, and individual spacecraft identification. In an Orion Artemis I example, one short-baseline S-band fit produced 54-ns TDOA and 0.8-Hz FDOA residual RMS, but the resulting orbit fit had 38.6-km RMS error relative to a reference orbit. That distinction illustrates why measurement residuals and state error must be reported separately. ([Safran WeTrack study](https://amostech.com/TechnicalPapers/2024/Cislunar_SDA/Thevenot.pdf))

In a simulated LRO campaign using regional ground-station clusters, passive-RF measurements covered an average of 71% of the orbit. At the fit date, the 0.95-quantile position error fell from 3,615.6 m for short baselines to 114.8 m for long baselines, and the maximum pointing-error quantile fell from 2.38 arcsec to 0.12 arcsec. Long-baseline performance required common visibility; when that geometry was unavailable, the system reverted to short baselines.

The passive-RF layer should therefore report:

- emitter detectability and signal availability;
- baseline geometry;
- synchronization uncertainty;
- TDOA and FDOA covariance;
- atmospheric and ionospheric corrections;
- whether the target is radiating through a main lobe or sidelobe;
- whether the result is an independent state estimate or only an association cue.

### DSN radiometrics, telemetry, and crosslinks are powerful but cooperative

NASA’s DSN has complexes at Goldstone, Madrid, and Canberra, with strategically separated long-baseline sites that allow another complex to acquire a signal as Earth rotates. Each complex includes a 70-m antenna, a 26-m antenna, and multiple 34-m antennas. NASA describes DSN support as continuous for deep-space, lunar, Lagrange-point, and highly elliptical-orbit missions, but the network is heavily subscribed and its geometry is Earth-centered. ([NASA Deep Space Network](https://www.nasa.gov/communicating-with-missions/dsn/))

The DSN should be treated as a high-quality cooperative tracking layer, not as a complete non-cooperative surveillance system. A 2021 NRHO study identifies DSN scheduling constraints, limited out-of-plane geometry, and poor applicability to non-cooperative vehicles. ([Journal of the Astronautical Sciences NRHO observability study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40295-021-00283-y))

Telemetry can reveal a spacecraft’s health, mode, intent, and maneuver timing, but only when the spacecraft or operator provides it. It should be integrated as a privileged identity and behavior source, not used to represent the whole target population.

Crosslink and onboard navigation reduce exclusive dependence on Earth. CAPSTONE’s CAPS experiment measures range and range-rate to NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and uses those measurements to estimate CAPSTONE’s position. The experiment was designed to supplement, not replace, two-way DSN navigation. ([NASA CAPSTONE mission page](https://www.nasa.gov/smallspacecraft/capstone/); [CAPSTONE navigation study](https://www.ion.org/publications/abstract.cfm?articleID=18208))

### Use distributed observer locations for geometric diversity

A broad architecture should combine:

- Earth-based optical and passive-RF sites;
- DSN and other deep-space radiometric assets;
- lunar-surface optical, infrared, and radar sites;
- lunar-orbit observers;
- L1/L2, halo, Lyapunov, DRO, or other cislunar observers;
- cooperative mission crosslinks;
- distributed communication and processing nodes.

The reason is not simply coverage area. Different observer locations change the measurement geometry, the occultation pattern, and the uncertainty direction that can be resolved.

A simulated Moon-based architecture of four mid-latitude narrow-field angles-only observers maintained 100% track custody for the study’s 15 target trajectories and produced average position RSS error below 1 km. Adding one space-based angles-only observer reduced average position-estimation RSS error by a factor of five, and the best combinations included both Moon-based and space-based angle and range measurements. These are CR3BP/UKF simulation results using selected target families, not flight acceptance thresholds. ([Koblick and Choi](https://amostech.com/TechnicalPapers/2022/Poster/Koblick_2.pdf))

Lunar surface sensors have fixed locations, no atmospheric turbulence, no platform orbit-determination burden, and potentially favorable thermal and power environments. They also have local horizon limits and cannot see the entire lunar vicinity from one site. The 2021 NRHO study found that three lunar-surface observatories were needed to view a full 9:2 NRHO because of the low perilune and surface horizon constraints. ([Journal of the Astronautical Sciences NRHO observability study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40295-021-00283-y))

### Calibration, time, and reference frames are architecture-level functions

Every sensor measurement should carry:

- acquisition time and time-scale definition;
- clock uncertainty and synchronization source;
- observer position and velocity with covariance;
- attitude and boresight calibration;
- instrument configuration and processing version;
- atmospheric, ionospheric, or media corrections;
- measurement covariance and quality flags;
- target signature or photometric metadata;
- reference frame and transformation pedigree.

The Artemis I Orion navigation architecture illustrates why these details matter. Orion used three inertial measurement units, two GPS receivers, two star trackers, one optical-navigation camera, and four extended Kalman filters. Outside low Earth orbit, the cislunar filter used a 21-state multiplicative-error model including position, velocity, attitude error, unmodeled acceleration, accelerometer biases and scale factors, and optical-sensor biases. ([Holt, D’Souza, and Wasinger](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20230000714/downloads/AAS-23-057_Artemis_1_Navigation_HoltDsouzaWasinger_FINALfinal.pdf))

Orion’s optical navigation used star-tracker quaternions and planet-centroid angles, with apparent diameter providing range. Earth’s atmosphere introduced a significant range-dependent bias; lunar terrain contributed more noise than bias. Software limitations forced common constant noise and bias parameters for Earth and Moon, which made the tuning conservative. Star trackers also downmoded when illuminated reaction-control plumes from Thruster 3 or Thruster 8 dazzled them.

A lunar-orbit OD study similarly warns that an analytic 0.1° lunar-libration accuracy corresponds to about 3 km at the lunar surface and is unsuitable for precision orbit determination. In its LRO comparison, the SDS solution produced about 8 m RMS versus 83 m for an Orekit configuration. ([Safran WeTrack study](https://amostech.com/TechnicalPapers/2024/Cislunar_SDA/Thevenot.pdf))

### Use SPICE and ephemerides as shared geometry infrastructure

NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE provides spacecraft and body ephemerides, instrument geometry, orientation, events, frames, time conversions, and shape models through documented kernel types. Its geometric-event-finder APIs can calculate ranges, lighting angles, occultations, and times when geometric parameters cross specified limits. ([NAIF SPICE concepts](https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/naif/spiceconcept.html))

A common geometry service should use SPICE or an equivalent pedigree-controlled system to generate:

- observer and target states;
- Earth, Moon, and Sun geometry;
- occultation and eclipse windows;
- illumination and phase angles;
- sensor exclusion angles;
- field-of-view intersections;
- frame and time transformations;
- event predictions for tasking.

The service should version its kernels and preserve the exact kernel set used to generate every catalog prediction. JPL DE430 was fitted simultaneously to lunar laser ranging and planetary data and included improved gravity, tidal, and asteroid perturbation models. Its uncertainty discussion also warns that internal quoted uncertainties exclude contributions from fixed parameters and theoretical conversion errors. ([DE430 lunar and planetary ephemeris memorandum](https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/pub/naif/generic_kernels/spk/planets/de430_moon_coord.pdf))

## 4. Turn measurements into an uncertainty-aware catalog

### Detection and track initiation

The front end should maintain separate streams for:

- thresholded detections;
- candidate detections below the normal threshold;
- non-detections within a predicted field of regard;
- tracklets;
- uncorrelated tracks;
- known-object updates.

For a bright or cooperative target, two or three measurements may be sufficient to initiate a provisional track. For an unknown faint object, track-before-detect or multi-frame integration may be necessary. Track initiation should preserve alternative hypotheses instead of forcing a single state too early.

Angles-only initial orbit determination is especially difficult in cislunar space because range and range-rate are initially weakly observed. The 2025 sparse-grid-collocation IOD study notes that conventional IOD can fail when gaps are measured in days or even hours. Its collocation formulation reconstructs a full non-Keplerian trajectory over a discretized grid and reports a larger convergence region without a close initial guess. Its periodic-IOD extension estimates a repeating orbit and natural period simultaneously from angles-only measurements. ([Non-Keplerian IOD with sparse-grid collocation](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40295-025-00491-w))

Before a full state and covariance exist, ordinary covariance-based association is unavailable. Heidrich and Holzinger instead use cislunar admissible-region constraints on range and range-rate, bounded using the Jacobi constant and two-body orbital energy relative to Earth and Moon. These constraints can be enforced at every measurement epoch in a nonlinear program. ([Heidrich and Holzinger](https://amostech.com/TechnicalPapers/2024/Cislunar_SDA/Heidrich.pdf))

The operational track-initiation record should include:

- all measurements used;
- measurements rejected and why;
- assumed measurement model;
- admissible range and range-rate interval;
- dynamic model and epoch;
- number of candidate hypotheses;
- initial covariance or ensemble;
- confidence that the track is real;
- next observation required to resolve the ambiguity.

### Measurement association and identity resolution

Association has three stages:

1. Associate a new measurement to an existing predicted track when the innovation is consistent with the track covariance and sensor detection model.
2. Associate independent tracklets when their feasible trajectories overlap under cislunar dynamics.
3. Associate the resulting track with an identity, mission, launch, operator record, or previously cataloged object.

For a mature track, the innovation should be tested against the predicted measurement covariance. For an uncorrelated track, use admissible regions, physical constraints, trajectory families, sensor signatures, photometry, RF behavior, and multiple hypotheses.

De Riz, Cipollone, and Di Lizia represent optical uncorrelated tracks as attributables containing angles and angular rates. Their correlation method propagates uncertainty through a CR3BP-based minimum-energy optimal-control problem and applies Mahalanobis-distance and Z-score screens. They use a fourth-order conjugate unscented transform because the simulated control-effort distribution is not strictly Gaussian, although its first two moments can be captured. ([De Riz, Cipollone, and Di Lizia](https://re.public.polimi.it/retrieve/705ed94d-d843-494f-bff8-6e01c12c265f/DERIA01-25.pdf))

Identity resolution should never rely only on an external identifier. A robust identity record should combine:

- operator-provided identifiers;
- launch and deployment relationships;
- predicted state and covariance;
- optical and photometric signature;
- RF frequency, modulation, and behavior;
- size and radar cross-section estimates;
- maneuver history;
- mission timeline;
- crosslink or telemetry confirmation;
- correlation evidence from independent sources.

TraCSS provides a useful governance pattern: its records are JSON, contain source and edit metadata, associate fields with source authority, redaction policy, and edit workflow, and require approval for edits to sensitive identifiers such as NORAD ID. Its object-type categories include Payload, Debris, Rocket Body, Unknown, and Other. ([TraCSS Cat specification](https://space.commerce.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/TraCSS-SPEC-003-TraCSS-Cat-Format-v2.0.5.pdf))

That governance is not yet a complete cislunar identity solution. A 2023 TraCSS standards paper states that satellite identification has no specific CCSDS standard and that data-sharing and public-sharing levels had not yet been determined. ([TraCSS standards recommendations](https://www.space.commerce.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023-Recommendations-TraCSS-Standards-for-Data-Exchange.pdf))

### Select the estimator according to the uncertainty regime

No single estimator is best across cislunar search, custody, maneuvering, and multi-object tracking.

| Estimation method | Best use | Advantage | Limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Batch least squares | Cooperative or well-associated arcs with many observations | Uses an entire arc and can estimate dynamic parameters and biases | Requires an initial association and can be computationally expensive or sensitive to local minima |
| Sparse collocation and nonlinear programming | Long gaps, periodic IOD, large maneuvers, weak initial guesses | Enforces dynamics over the whole arc and can estimate control history | Large nonlinear programs and measurement-association complexity |
| EKF | Fast sequential updates with a reasonably local Gaussian state | Low latency and mature implementation | Linearization can fail under strong nonlinearity, gaps, or multimodal uncertainty |
| UKF and sigma-point filters | Nonlinear sequential tracking with moderate state dimension | Better nonlinear measurement and propagation treatment than a first-order EKF | Still approximates the distribution as Gaussian and can become inconsistent under severe nonlinearity |
| Information filters and EIF-based methods | Predictive multi-sensor tasking and distributed fusion | Measurement information is additive and can reduce assignment-history dependence | Requires careful information management and still depends on the underlying model |
| IMM, Gaussian mixtures, and AGMIMM | Maneuvering or mode-uncertain targets | Represents ballistic and maneuver modes simultaneously | Exact mode histories grow exponentially; reduction is approximate |
| Labeled multi-Bernoulli and related random-finite-set filters | Multiple unknown objects and cardinality uncertainty | Jointly estimates object states and the number of objects | More complex implementation and dependence on an adequate detection and clutter model |
| Monte Carlo or particle ensembles | Non-Gaussian prediction and validation | Captures curved, split, and heavy-tailed distributions | Computationally expensive, especially for many targets and long horizons |

Chow et al. report that a UKF performed relatively well across several orbit families and observation cadences, while Gaussian-mixture methods showed promise during large data gaps. Their data-fusion study found that passive RF measurements primarily helped by filling gaps in electro-optical observations. The measurements and networks were synthetic, so these findings support architecture choices rather than operational thresholds. ([Chow et al.](https://amostech.space/year/2022/cislunar-orbit-determination-improvements-in-uncertainty-realism-and-data-fusion/))

The AGMIMM filter addresses ballistic and maneuvering cooperative or non-cooperative objects by estimating both kinematic state and maneuver modality. Its demonstration uses synthetic angles-only measurements and CR3BP assumptions. It explicitly assimilates non-detections as negative information when the target was inside the field of view, illuminated, unocculted, and outside the lunar exclusion cone. That is operationally important: a missed detection should update a track only when the sensor’s probability of detection was sufficiently high. ([AGMIMM cislunar tracking study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40295-024-00478-z))

### Maneuver and behavior-change detection

A maneuver detector should combine:

- innovation and normalized-innovation-squared monitoring;
- adaptive process-noise estimation;
- IMM or maneuver-mode filters;
- trajectory re-fit with impulsive and finite-burn hypotheses;
- photometric or RF behavior changes;
- operator and telemetry reports;
- non-detection patterns inconsistent with the nominal model.

A 2021 cislunar maneuver study used an optimal-control-based estimator and a binary hypothesis test. For a simulated impulse policy with a 50-mm/s mean and 15-mm/s standard deviation, it correctly identified maneuver occurrence in 194 of 200 tests. ([Journal of the Astronautical Sciences maneuver study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40295-021-00283-y))

A separate passive-RF simulation evaluated 528 cases. Its maneuver-detection rate approached 100% above 1 m/s, but detection depended on maneuver direction: cross-track maneuvers were easier to detect than radial maneuvers. Very large maneuvers could cause the filter to lose track, so maneuver detection and custody recovery must be measured separately. ([Wetterer et al.](https://amostech.com/TechnicalPapers/2022/Poster/Wetterer.pdf))

A 2026 modal-innovation study detects maneuvers through spikes in reduced-order normalized innovation sequences and proposes covariance inflation after detection. In a simulated 9:2 Gateway-like NRHO case with a 10-m/s maneuver, a 90th-percentile threshold produced an approximately 10% nominal false-positive rate, consistent with the selected theoretical threshold. This is a simulation result, not a recommended operational false-alarm setting. ([Modal innovation maneuver detection study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40295-026-00604-z))

Fedeler, Holzinger, and Whitacre use a lagging horizon of five observations to trigger adaptive process-noise evaluation. Such a horizon can be useful for rapid response, but it should be tuned to the target’s dynamics and sensor cadence rather than adopted as a universal value. ([Sensor tasking in the cislunar regime](https://d1io3yog0oux5.cloudfront.net/_d14d0599049bb08e92930e2b28602521/draper/db/2545/24078/document/maneuver_journal_%281%29.pdf))

### Propagate covariance and model uncertainty, not just a nominal trajectory

A nominal state is inadequate for sensor scheduling and safety decisions. The operational prediction should be represented as either:

- a mean state and covariance that has passed consistency checks;
- a Gaussian mixture;
- a sigma-point set;
- a Monte Carlo ensemble;
- or another explicitly documented non-Gaussian representation.

A generic model can be written as \(\dot{x}=f(x,t,u,\theta)+w\), \(y=h(x,t)+v\), where \(x\) is the state, \(u\) includes known or hypothesized maneuvers, \(\theta\) includes uncertain model parameters, and \(w\) and \(v\) represent process and measurement errors.

The catalog should propagate uncertainty through the same dynamic and frame models used to propagate the state. It should not accept a covariance generated under a two-body model and silently apply it to an Earth–Moon–Sun model.

Consistency should be assessed with innovation tests such as \(NIS=\nu^{T}S^{-1}\nu\) and truth-based validation with \(NEES=e^{T}P^{-1}e\), where \(\nu\) is the measurement innovation, \(S\) its predicted covariance, \(e\) the state error, and \(P\) the estimated state covariance. These statistics should be stratified by target class, sensor, geometry, and prediction horizon.

### Use cislunar-appropriate ephemeris products

Classical TLEs and SGP4 are not adequate as the primary representation for many cislunar trajectories. The AFRL primer recommends sharing an instantaneous position and velocity vector in an agreed inertial frame at a known epoch rather than relying on TLEs or classical orbital elements. The proposed cislunar message set similarly recommends transmitting ephemerides with covariances propagated over the desired interval, rather than requiring every recipient to reproduce the producer’s dynamics and numerical models. ([AFRL cislunar primer](https://www.afrl.af.mil/Portals/90/Documents/RV/A%20Primer%20on%20Cislunar%20Space_Dist%20A_PA2021-1271.pdf?ver=vs6e0sE4PuJ51QC-15DEfg%3D%3D); [proposed cislunar SSA message set](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/cislunar_ssa_proposed_message_set-nov2021_rev2_without_emailspdf.pdf))

The product hierarchy should use named, interoperable formats:

- OPM for a state vector at a specified epoch;
- OEM for a history or forecast of state vectors;
- OCM for orbit data combined with additional spacecraft and environmental information;
- TDM for tracking measurements;
- CDM for conjunction data;
- RDM where applicable for re-entry or related navigation data;
- SPICE SPK and related kernels for precision geometry and mission operations;
- a cislunar propagated-ephemeris product containing covariance and model metadata.

The CCSDS XML Navigation Data Message specification defines OPM, OMM, OEM, OCM, TDM, CDM, and RDM schemas, but it does not define the transmission method. That requires a separate interface-control agreement. ([CCSDS XML Navigation Data Messages](https://ccsds.org/Pubs/505x0b3e2.pdf))

A cislunar record should contain, at minimum:

- immutable internal object identifier;
- external identifiers and aliases;
- object type and identity confidence;
- owner, operator, and mission status;
- state epoch, time scale, frame, and position/velocity;
- covariance or ensemble definition;
- dynamic model and force-model version;
- maneuver history and maneuver hypotheses;
- observation history and provenance;
- last valid observation and state age;
- predicted event times and uncertainty;
- sensor detection and non-detection statistics;
- source authority, classification, redaction, and edit history;
- superseded and successor record links.

Operational catalog versioning and cross-agency deduplication remain unresolved in the supplied evidence. A sound implementation should therefore treat every update as a versioned hypothesis with explicit provenance rather than overwrite a previous state without a change record.

## 5. Operate a closed-loop short-term tracking system

The short-term mission is not simply to collect observations at a fixed cadence. It is to decide what information is most valuable next, collect it before uncertainty or risk becomes unacceptable, reprocess the track, and pass a usable decision product to the next operator or sensor.

### 1. Ingest observations and assess their quality

The system should first normalize all measurements into a common time and frame system, apply calibration and media corrections, attach measurement covariance, and check residuals against sensor-specific quality limits.

A measurement should be rejected, down-weighted, or retained as a separate hypothesis when:

- timing or clock quality is insufficient;
- the observer state is stale;
- a boresight or attitude anomaly is active;
- the target is near an exclusion boundary;
- the signal is below the calibrated detection regime;
- the measurement residual is inconsistent with the track;
- a known event, such as a thruster firing or eclipse, can explain the error.

Artemis I demonstrates why the quality state must accompany the measurement. Orion’s optical-navigation passes were accepted only when residuals and covariances met a preselected criterion. Some star-tracker outages were later correlated with thruster plume events. ([Holt, D’Souza, and Wasinger](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20230000714/downloads/AAS-23-057_Artemis_1_Navigation_HoltDsouzaWasinger_FINALfinal.pdf))

### 2. Select targets using risk, uncertainty, novelty, and custody margin

A practical target-selection policy should preserve both safety and discovery capacity. A useful priority state includes:

- predicted conjunction or miss-distance risk;
- covariance growth rate;
- time to the next occultation or critical event;
- probability of maneuver or behavior change;
- mission criticality;
- target novelty and identity uncertainty;
- current track age and handoff margin;
- sensor availability and expected information gain;
- whether an operator-supplied ephemeris is stale or absent;
- whether the target is part of the unknown-object search quota.

A high-risk known target should not consume all available resources. Unknown-object search must remain active because an apparently complete cooperative catalog does not cover non-cooperative debris or unreported spacecraft.

No common cislunar policy establishes numerical thresholds for these factors. Mission planners should define target classes and escalation levels in the CONOPS, then report the thresholds with every evaluation.

### 3. Generate predictions and observation windows

For each candidate target, propagate a state distribution through the current high-fidelity model. Generate observation windows using:

- field of view and pointing limits;
- Earth and Moon occultation;
- Sun and Moon exclusion angles;
- illumination and thermal conditions;
- local horizon and weather;
- target range and predicted signal-to-noise;
- station availability and communications latency;
- expected uncertainty at the time of observation.

A window should be defined over a probability region, not only the nominal trajectory. If the 3-sigma or ensemble search region is larger than the sensor field of view, the task should include a scan pattern or a decision about which portion of the uncertainty distribution is most valuable.

SPICE geometric-event finder APIs are suitable for generating occultation, lighting, range, and boundary-crossing events, provided that the kernels and frame definitions are version controlled. ([NAIF SPICE concepts](https://naif.jpl.nasa.gov/naif/spiceconcept.html))

### 4. Choose a tasking policy appropriate to the decision horizon

Several tasking alternatives are useful, but their performance is configuration-dependent.

| Policy | What it does | Evidence and benefit | Limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Uniform cadence | Revisits all targets at fixed intervals | Simple, robust to modeling errors, useful as a baseline | Wastes resources on low-risk targets and misses geometry-specific opportunities |
| Reactive or myopic | Selects the best immediate observation | Low computation and quick response to a new detection | Can sacrifice future coverage or walk into a predicted occultation gap |
| Predictive rolling horizon | Optimizes several future steps and replans repeatedly | Tomita et al. use rolling-horizon ILP for changing demand; predictive methods have outperformed myopic methods in some metrics | Depends on demand, dynamics, and model quality; exact optimization can be expensive |
| Information-gain tasking | Selects measurements expected to reduce covariance or entropy | Useful for separating targets and shrinking uncertainty; one study uses trace of inverse covariance | Information gain alone may neglect mission risk, discovery, or latency |
| Distributed auction or consensus | Sensors exchange local bids and assignments | Supports heterogeneous sensors and degraded central control; BACC studies combine auctions with uncertainty-based assignments | Requires communications and can make globally suboptimal decisions |
| MCTS or other tree search | Explores future task sequences and maneuver-aware branches | Fedeler et al. report robustness against stationkeeping and injection-error cases | Computational complexity; their maneuver events were not inserted inside the tree search |
| Joint constellation and tasking | Chooses observer locations and pointing schedule together | TE-p-MP and related MILP methods recognize that architecture and tasking are coupled | Discretization and scale; one TE-p-MP formulation contains on the order of \(10^{6}\) variables |

The 2025 concurrent phasing and tasking study separates observer phasing from inner-loop tasking and uses an information objective based on the trace of the inverse covariance. In one intersecting-orbit case, myopic control came within 1% of optimal control, making the extra computation difficult to justify. The same study reports larger benefits for predictive control when favorable close approaches are absent. ([Concurrent phasing and tasking study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40295-025-00520-8))

A separate predictive-tasking study using an extended information filter reports that predictive tasking outperformed myopic tasking in two metrics, but explicitly states that the result depends on the formulation. ([Predictive multi-observer tasking study](https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2310.04894v1))

The resulting policy should be hybrid:

- use risk and custody margin to establish mandatory tasks;
- use information gain to choose among safe alternatives;
- use predictive scheduling around occultations, perilune, and conjunction events;
- reserve capacity for search and unknowns;
- replan after every high-value measurement or maneuver indication.

### 5. Execute adaptive revisit and event-triggered monitoring

The revisit interval should be driven by the predicted uncertainty at the next decision point, not by a universal clock. Revisit urgency rises when:

- covariance expands toward or beyond a protected region;
- the target approaches perilune or a close-approach geometry;
- a sensor handoff is approaching;
- the track enters a Sun, Earth, or Moon exclusion interval;
- a non-detection conflicts with the predicted detection probability;
- an innovation spike suggests a maneuver;
- identity hypotheses diverge;
- a new object appears near a known mission.

Negative information is valuable only when the sensor should probably have detected the target. A missed observation during lunar occultation carries no evidence against the track. A missed observation inside a high-probability field of view with good sensitivity can lower the probability of the current hypothesis or trigger a search expansion.

### 6. Transfer custody explicitly between sensors

A handoff should occur while two sensors have overlapping predicted access, not after the primary sensor loses the target. The handoff process should:

1. propagate the current state distribution to the overlap window;
2. identify sensors with suitable geometry, sensitivity, and availability;
3. send the predicted search region and measurement model to the receiving sensor;
4. collect a confirmation measurement or a documented non-detection;
5. compare the new measurement with the predicted distribution;
6. promote the receiving sensor to primary custody only after association quality passes the handoff criterion;
7. retain the original sensor’s track and provenance for later reconciliation.

Correa et al.’s ICON architecture evaluates sensor position, imaging capability, physical occlusions, and tasking freedom before recommending pointing or local search. It regenerates tasks after a new track update and increases cadence when association ambiguity is high. Its raster search was bounded by a 3-sigma covariance ellipse, but the raster did not model the probability distribution inside that ellipse. ([ICON adaptive tasking study](https://amostech.com/TechnicalPapers/2024/Poster/Correa.pdf))

### 7. Reprocess rapidly after new data or maneuvers

A new measurement should trigger the smallest sufficient reprocessing action:

- ordinary sequential update if the association is clear and the residual is nominal;
- a recent-window batch update if the track is inconsistent;
- a lagged-horizon reprocessing if process noise or maneuver probability rises;
- a multi-hypothesis trajectory refit if maneuver time, duration, or magnitude is uncertain;
- full tracklet re-association if the target may have been lost;
- cross-catalog correlation if an identity conflict appears.

The system should retain the pre-update state, post-update state, and reason for the change. This is essential for operator trust and for distinguishing a real maneuver from a sensor or model failure.

No common measured observation-to-track, maneuver-reprocessing, or alert latency was established in the supplied evidence. These latencies must be measured end to end in representative operational tests rather than inferred from sensor cadence or communications bandwidth.

### 8. Publish alerts and define task completion

An alert should contain:

- object identifier and identity alternatives;
- last observation and track age;
- current and predicted state;
- covariance or ensemble summary;
- event time and uncertainty;
- detection and association confidence;
- maneuver or behavior-change evidence;
- sensor and source provenance;
- recommended next observation;
- operator acknowledgment state;
- consequences of delayed action.

Alert escalation should be tied to the decision supported. A predicted collision, loss of custody, unexpected maneuver, or unknown object near a crewed mission may require different thresholds.

A proposed task-completion criterion can require all of the following:

- the requested measurement was attempted;
- the target was detected, or a sensitivity-qualified non-detection was recorded;
- the measurement was associated or left as an explicit alternative;
- the updated covariance passed consistency checks;
- the next custody owner accepted the track;
- the resulting product was published within the task latency budget;
- any required alert was acknowledged.

These are operational design criteria, not common cislunar standards.

## 6. Measure effectiveness with scenario-specific metrics

### Core performance measures

| Measure | Definition | Necessary qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Probability of detection | Detected opportunities divided by truth opportunities | Report by target size, signature, range, illumination, geometry, and sensor |
| Probability of recognition or identification | Correct classifications or identity resolutions divided by valid recognition opportunities | Separate object type recognition from exact identity resolution |
| False-alarm rate | False detections per look, resolution cell, or search volume | State the denominator and detector threshold |
| False-track rate | Spurious tracks that survive initiation criteria or enter the catalog | Keep separate from single-look false alarms |
| Catalog completeness | Truth objects with valid catalog products divided by the declared reference population | State whether the denominator includes unknowns and RF-silent objects |
| Track continuity | Custodial time or required updates completed without an unresolved gap | Report longest gap and gap distribution, not only an average |
| State accuracy | Position and velocity error at specified epochs | Separate current-state error from predicted-state error |
| Covariance consistency | Fraction of truth errors contained within stated uncertainty bounds | Report NIS, NEES, or empirical coverage |
| Latency | Time from event or measurement to usable track, reprocessed state, or alert | Include queueing, communications, and operator delay |
| Coverage and revisit | Fraction of target-time or region-time satisfying the requirement and distribution of revisit intervals | Do not substitute time-averaged area for target custody |
| Resource efficiency | Accuracy, coverage, or risk reduction per sensor, observation, energy, bandwidth, or operator action | Include reserve capacity and degraded modes |
| Robustness | Performance retained under outages, model error, weather, illumination, link loss, or sensor failure | Report the failure scenario and recovery time |

For a detection experiment, use \(P_d=N_{\mathrm{detected}}/N_{\mathrm{opportunities}}\). For catalog completeness, use \(C=N_{\mathrm{valid\ products}}/N_{\mathrm{truth\ population}}\). Both are meaningful only when the opportunities and truth population are explicitly defined.

False alarms and false tracks must not be conflated. A false alarm is a detector-level event. A false track is a sequence of false or misassociated measurements that survives track initiation and may consume tasking resources or enter the catalog. The supplied evidence does not provide a validated populated-catalog false-track rate for cislunar operations.

### What existing studies can and cannot demonstrate

Several results provide useful benchmarks, but they are not directly comparable:

- DeCoster et al. model 95% detection probability and 10⁻⁴ false-alarm probability for a large RCS target under a specified active-RF design. The result is a per-look model, not a populated-catalog operational false-track measurement.
- Koblick and Choi simulate 100% custody and below-1-km average position RSS error for a four-observer lunar architecture. The target set contains 15 selected periodic trajectories and uses CR3BP and a UKF.
- The WeTrack study reports passive-RF measurement residuals, coverage, and simulated Monte Carlo covariance validation, but its Orion example is cooperative and its LRO performance depends strongly on baseline geometry.
- The 2021 optical study found that angle-only filtering from a single L2 observer diverged before periapsis for tested cadences from one minute to 12 hours, while adding angular-rate measurements produced consistent filtering in every simulated scenario. Its selected 9:2 NRHO case used a 2-hour cadence as a low-demand balance. ([Journal of the Astronautical Sciences NRHO observability study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40295-021-00283-y))
- Wetterer et al. report near-100% maneuver detection above 1 m/s in 528 synthetic cases, but high-delta-v cases could lose track.
- Spaceflux reports an independent optical campaign during cooperative Artemis II operations in which seven sensors across four continents collected 1,736 calibrated measurements of Orion and the ICPS. Its New Mexico and Western Australia sensors independently confirmed Orion’s inbound trajectory within seven minutes. This demonstrates distributed optical operations and rapid confirmation for a known mission, not non-cooperative catalog completeness. ([Spaceflux Artemis II campaign](https://spaceflux.io/an-independent-optical-record-of-the-first-crewed-lunar-mission-since-apollo-17/))
- CisLunarSense predicts 700-km detection for low-relative-velocity Gateway debris and 400–630 km for modeled external threats, but its relay waveform and processing assumptions are not yet the current operational HLCS baseline.
- DeCoster’s 65% search coverage, 50–92% passive-RF detection coverage, and 58–75% recognition coverage arise from a 30-day, two-dimensional, architecture-level simulation with representative targets and effective apertures. They are not measurements of a deployed network.

The correct use of these results is to populate a validation matrix and expose trade-offs, not to select one figure as a universal cislunar requirement.

### Validation scenarios should cover the full operating envelope

A serious validation campaign should include at least the following scenarios.

| Scenario | Required stress | Primary measures |
|---|---|---|
| Cooperative NRHO | CAPSTONE- or Gateway-like target, DSN plus crosslink or onboard navigation, occultation and perilune | State accuracy, covariance consistency, handoff latency, one-revolution prediction |
| Crewed translunar mission | Orion-like optical navigation, DSN outages, attitude or star-tracker interruptions, deployment of secondary payloads | Track continuity, outage recovery, identity association, alert latency |
| Non-cooperative L1/L2 target | Angles-only optical, passive RF when available, weak range diversity, alternate observer orbits | IOD convergence, association probability, false-track rate, uncertainty growth |
| Lunar-orbit population | Low and highly elliptical lunar orbits, lunar gravity harmonics, surface occultation, multi-target tasking | Revisit, prediction error, conjunction probability sensitivity, resource efficiency |
| Translunar transfer corridor | Known and unknown low-energy and higher-energy transfers, time-varying transit region | Search completeness, discovery latency, track initiation, corridor coverage |
| Maneuver and fragmentation | Small station keeping, radial and cross-track impulses, large maneuvers, debris clouds | Maneuver-detection probability, reprocessing latency, track recovery, cardinality |
| Illumination and environmental gaps | Eclipse, lunar and Earth occultation, Sun exclusion, optical background, weather | Detection probability conditioned on opportunity, gap duration, recovery |
| Communications degradation | DSN or relay outage, delayed messages, intermittent crosslink, delayed catalog updates | Local autonomy, data freshness, alert latency, loss and recovery |
| Multi-organization exchange | Independent catalogs and sensor operators with different identifiers and models | Deduplication, provenance, version reconciliation, conflict resolution |

Truth should be generated independently of the estimator under test. The test should include held-out sensors and injected unknown objects, not merely replay the measurements used to construct the reference trajectory. Results should be stratified by regime, target class, observer location, illumination, and prediction lead time.

## 7. Mission and system lessons

### CAPSTONE: cooperative navigation and the value of crosslink measurements

CAPSTONE took approximately four months from launch to its NRHO insertion on 13 November 2022. Its operations team analyzed spacecraft data to confirm the expected orbit and conducted two cleanup maneuvers. NASA also reports communications and propulsion challenges during the transfer. ([NASA CAPSTONE mission page](https://www.nasa.gov/smallspacecraft/capstone/))

CAPSTONE’s CAPS experiment uses direct ranging with LRO: CAPSTONE measures distance to LRO and the rate of change of that distance, then uses the crosslink measurements for onboard navigation. The mission’s nominal architecture continued to rely on two-way DSN radiometrics, while CAPS was a technology demonstration intended to supplement ground navigation. High-fidelity simulations predicted single-kilometer position and single-centimeter-per-second velocity uncertainty for one-way uplink measurements, with crosslink performance similar to expected two-way tracking. ([CAPSTONE navigation study](https://www.ion.org/publications/abstract.cfm?articleID=18208))

The lesson is not that autonomous crosslink navigation eliminates the DSN. It is that a cislunar awareness architecture benefits from independent measurement paths. Crosslink observations can fill ground outages, reduce state age, and provide local geometry, while ground radiometrics provide absolute reference and operational oversight.

### Artemis I and Orion: sensor fusion, certification, and outage handling

Orion’s Artemis I navigation architecture combined inertial sensors, GPS, star trackers, optical navigation, DSN updates, and multiple filters. Outside low Earth orbit, its cislunar filter included unmodeled acceleration and optical-sensor biases, which is a useful operational example of including model and instrument uncertainty in the state rather than treating it as an afterthought.

Orion used two distinct state-update paths: ground-based DSN updates and onboard optical navigation. Before routine optical passes, Orion calibrated the camera and star trackers by imaging stars, then imaged Earth or the Moon. Certification required a two-hour navigation pass and residual and covariance checks against a preselected criterion. Routine image-gathering passes lasted 15 minutes, and the distant-retrograde-orbit phase used daily 15-minute passes. ([Holt, D’Souza, and Wasinger](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20230000714/downloads/AAS-23-057_Artemis_1_Navigation_HoltDsouzaWasinger_FINALfinal.pdf))

The mission also demonstrates why a schedule cannot assume continuous sensor availability. NASA records a 47-minute unplanned loss of data between Orion and the DSN during Flight Day 8 and a planned communication gap of about 4.5 hours during Flight Day 18 while ground stations were reconfigured. Artemis I also deployed 10 CubeSats from an adapter attached to the SLS upper stage, with different signal-acquisition timelines for each spacecraft. ([Artemis I mission timeline](https://www.nasa.gov/reference/artemis-i-mission-timeline/))

The operational lessons are direct:

- include outages in the nominal test case;
- preserve independent navigation paths;
- treat secondary payloads and upper stages as separate catalog objects;
- maintain a track even when contact is temporarily lost;
- certify sensor passes through residual and covariance tests;
- model attitude and thruster events as possible measurement disturbances.

### The DSN is essential infrastructure, not a complete cislunar catalog

The DSN’s three-site geometry provides global access and continuity for cooperative missions. NASA’s DSN Now display is driven by real-time ground-station data and updates every five seconds, but it is not a schedule of planned communication sessions. This distinction matters when building a sensor-tasking system: real-time network status is not the same as future observation availability. ([NASA Deep Space Network](https://www.nasa.gov/communicating-with-missions/dsn/))

The DSN should therefore be integrated with an independent tasking service that knows:

- scheduled and possible DSN contacts;
- mission priority and cross-support rules;
- expected range and Doppler quality;
- station maintenance or reconfiguration;
- alternate optical, RF, or crosslink observations;
- communications latency from measurement to catalog.

### SPICE, JPL ephemerides, and the transition away from TLE-centric operations

The traditional Earth-orbit catalog model is not sufficient for cislunar operations. The field is moving toward state vectors, high-fidelity propagated ephemerides, covariance, and geometry kernels.

SPICE provides a shared framework for spacecraft and body geometry, while JPL DE430 and DE440 provide high-quality planetary and lunar ephemerides. The JPL Three-Body Periodic Orbit Catalog supports generation and comparison of CR3BP orbit families. These resources should be connected through a controlled reference-data service rather than individually embedded in sensor software.

The transition is operational as well as mathematical:

- from Earth-centered orbital elements to state vectors and ephemerides in declared frames;
