- from a single ground-navigation path to ground, onboard, crosslink, and distributed sensors;
- from fixed revisit to geometry- and uncertainty-driven tasking;
- from cooperative mission tracking to a mixed population containing unknown and non-cooperative objects;
- from isolated mission products to interoperable, provenance-aware catalogs.

### Standards and exchange mechanisms

| Standard or system | Main role | Cislunar use and limitation |
|---|---|---|
| CCSDS TDM | Measurement exchange for range, Doppler, angles, Delta-DOR, and related data | Useful foundation, but the fetched issue is historical and leaves accuracy and transmission details to an ICD |
| CCSDS TD-CSTS | Near-real-time transfer of TDM-formatted tracking measurements | Supports incremental delivery, but its real-time scope is limited mainly to signal- and angle-related fields |
| CCSDS XML Navigation Data Messages | XML schemas for OPM, OMM, OEM, OCM, TDM, CDM, and RDM | Provides message semantics; transmission and security arrangements remain external |
| TraCSS Cat | Multi-source catalog records and governance | Provides object types, source authorities, edit permissions, and validation; cislunar identity and sharing policies remain incomplete |
| Proposed cislunar SSA message set | Cislunar state, covariance, observation, signature, and propagated-ephemeris concepts | Recommends producer-propagated ephemerides and covariance but is a proposed architecture, not a settled operational standard |
| SPICE | Geometry, ephemerides, frames, clocks, events, and shape models | Strong mission-operations foundation when kernels are versioned and distributed with pedigree |
| LunaNet and DTN | Communications, navigation, timing, and delay-tolerant networking | Supports intermittent links and store-and-forward operations; service maturity and cross-organization deployment vary |

The 2007 CCSDS TDM was intended to cover approximately 95% of tracking scenarios, but it is explicitly a historical issue and relies on ICDs for details outside the standard’s scope. The 2023 TD-CSTS provides near-real-time tracking transfer as soon as a cross-support complex generates measurements, but excludes several data categories better suited to file transfer. ([CCSDS TDM](https://ccsds.org/Pubs/503x0b1s.pdf); [CCSDS TD-CSTS](https://ccsds.org/Pubs/922x2b2.pdf))

The proposed cislunar message set goes further by recommending covariance-propagated ephemerides rather than a single state and covariance that every recipient must independently propagate. This reduces dependence on identical force models and numerical implementations, but increases data volume and requires trust in the producer’s model and provenance. ([proposed cislunar SSA message set](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/cislunar_ssa_proposed_message_set-nov2021_rev2_without_emailspdf.pdf))

### TraCSS and the current catalog gap

TraCSS provides a significant catalog-governance development. Its specification says that data can be integrated from the Department of Defense, NASA-derived estimates, spacecraft operators, and national governments. It records source authority, edit permissions, redaction policy, and workflow. Its overview also describes owner/operator ephemerides, maneuver plans, conjunction notifications, and screening every four hours for its broader space-traffic-coordination function. ([TraCSS Cat specification](https://space.commerce.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/TraCSS-SPEC-003-TraCSS-Cat-Format-v2.0.5.pdf); [TraCSS overview](https://space.commerce.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/TraCSS-Overview-Presentation-May-2026.pdf))

These mechanisms should not be mistaken for a populated, passive cislunar debris catalog. A 2025 MITRE report states that lunar and deep-space conjunction assessment lacks an Earth-orbit-equivalent passive catalog and that NASA’s MADCAP depends on voluntary, self-reported ephemerides and uncertainties. The report describes GOLLD as a 2021 capability aimed at cataloging objects at lunar distance and ORACLE/CHPS as a capability listed for 2027 or later. This is a roadmap and operational-process assessment, not evidence that a comprehensive catalog already exists. ([MITRE Protecting Cislunar Space](https://www.mitre.org/sites/default/files/2025-09/Protecting-cislunar-space-PR-25-00216-12.pdf))

### Communications resilience must support delayed and degraded operations

A cislunar tracking network cannot assume continuous low-latency connectivity. NASA’s LunaNet concept and CCSDS Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking use store-and-forward principles to tolerate intermittent links, long delays, and bit errors. BP version 7 and custody transfer allow data to remain in a node until a path becomes available. CAPSTONE has hosted BPNode experiments at on-orbit rates as low as 2 Kbps, while laboratory tests reached almost 900 Mbps with large bundles; the laboratory result is not an on-orbit throughput result. ([Small Satellite Conference DTN abstract](https://digitalcommons.usu.edu/smallsat/2026/all2026/42/))

A 2025 cislunar DTN testbed used one-way delays from 1.25 to 5 seconds, three bit-error conditions, and 16 samples per protocol configuration. At zero bit error, it found that an LTP-over-LTP primary relay configuration had the highest simulated goodput across tested delays. This is a communications-protocol simulation, not a tracking-accuracy or alert-latency measurement. ([Cislunar DTN performance study](https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/25/1/195))

A resilient awareness system should implement:

- local catalog and tasking autonomy at each cislunar node;
- store-and-forward observation bundles;
- local alerts when Earth contact is unavailable;
- primary and backup processing centers;
- replicated kernels and catalog history;
- authenticated data provenance;
- replay protection and access control;
- cross-support procedures between organizations;
- graceful degradation when a sensor, link, or processing center fails.

The supplied evidence documents DTN, backup operations centers, and cross-support mechanisms, but does not provide direct validation against cyber attack, space-weather disruption, contested communications, or major infrastructure failure. Those cases must be included in validation rather than assumed away.

## 8. Remaining implementation constraints and technical gaps

### Data sharing and identity remain as important as sensing

A sensor network can observe an object without being able to identify it, and an operator can possess a highly accurate ephemeris without sharing it. The operational system must support multiple levels of data release:

- full precision for trusted mission and safety partners;
- covariance and maneuver information for conjunction assessment;
- reduced or redacted products for broader coordination;
- observation signatures and association clues where state data cannot be shared;
- signed provenance and version history for every release.

The identity exchange must support aliases, unresolved conflicts, object splits and merges, deployment relationships, and changes in mission status. The absence of a settled CCSDS satellite-identification standard and unresolved public-sharing provisions are direct interoperability gaps. ([TraCSS standards recommendations](https://www.space.commerce.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023-Recommendations-TraCSS-Standards-for-Data-Exchange.pdf))

### Sparse data and model error require explicit uncertainty budgets

The largest operational mistakes will often arise from understated uncertainty rather than from a visibly noisy measurement. Every product should distinguish:

- measurement error;
- observer-state error;
- frame and clock error;
- dynamic-model error;
- maneuver uncertainty;
- SRP and attitude uncertainty;
- unmodeled fragmentation or deployment;
- association and identity uncertainty;
- communications age and delay.

For non-cooperative targets, covariance should not be artificially reduced merely because a filter has converged numerically. A model-consistency monitor should inflate uncertainty or branch hypotheses when residuals, maneuver indicators, or non-detections show that the current model is no longer credible.

### Scalability is a systems problem

Cislunar scale affects not only sensors but also computation and communications. The TE-p-MP study treats constellation placement and pointing as a coupled problem and reports approximately \(10^{6}\) decision variables for its time-expanded formulation. It uses Lagrangian relaxation and custom heuristics to obtain feasible solutions rapidly, while generic branch-and-bound performance varies substantially by problem difficulty. ([Cislunar SSA constellation design and planning](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.06238v4))

The operational implication is to separate decisions by timescale:

- strategic: choose orbit families, sensor locations, and communication architecture;
- tactical: schedule target groups and transfer corridors over days or weeks;
- operational: assign pointing and revisits over minutes or hours;
- immediate: resolve detections, maneuvers, and handoffs.

A single monolithic optimizer is unlikely to be appropriate for every decision. A hierarchical system can use fast heuristics for immediate tasking, predictive optimization for high-value campaigns, and slower joint design tools for constellation planning.

### Acceptance thresholds should be declared, not inferred

The collision-risk literature provides examples of mission-specific thresholds, not universal cislunar standards. Crum, Gunter, and Borowitz simulate six current lunar satellites and approximately 50 future objects using high-fidelity dynamics. They report that operators in their study treated collision probabilities of \(10^{-7}\) or \(10^{-6}\) as exceeding their risk threshold and estimate that a 50-satellite LLO fleet could require up to four avoidance maneuvers per satellite per year. They also show that perceived collision-risk counts depend strongly on covariance size. ([Cislunar Orbit Collision Probability Analysis](https://doi.org/10.2514/1.a36114))

Those values should not be copied into every mission. They demonstrate why the awareness system must report covariance quality and why better tracking can reduce both false alarms and unnecessary avoidance maneuvers.

### Space-weather and cyber resilience need direct testing

The network should test:

- RF link degradation and scintillation;
- optical background and thermal changes;
- timing loss;
- loss of a DSN complex or lunar relay;
- sensor spoofing or false data injection;
- corrupted or delayed ephemeris exchange;
- compromised catalog identifiers;
- denial of service against tasking or alert distribution;
- failure of primary and backup processing centers;
- conflicting measurements from independent organizations.

The supplied evidence supports the use of redundant sensors, DTN, backup operations centers, cross-support standards, and provenance metadata. It does not establish measured resilience under all of these threats. The correct operational posture is therefore to treat resilience as an unvalidated requirement until tested.

## Closing judgment

The most accurate present-day answer is a closed-loop, multi-phenomenology cislunar awareness network built around five principles:

1. Declare the region, target population, time horizon, and performance denominator before claiming completeness.
2. Use diverse observer locations and measurements because optical visibility, RF availability, and dynamic observability vary by target and phase.
3. Replace TLE-centric handling with high-fidelity, frame-controlled ephemerides, covariance or ensembles, and versioned provenance.
4. Select and retask sensors using risk, covariance growth, event geometry, information gain, and protected search capacity.
5. Judge effectiveness with detection, identification, continuity, state accuracy, covariance consistency, latency, coverage, false-track, resource, and resilience measures in scenario-specific tests.

CAPSTONE, Artemis I, Orion, the DSN, SPICE, lunar and cislunar sensor studies, DTN, and TraCSS show that the necessary pieces are developing. They do not yet constitute a universal cislunar catalog or a validated common operating standard. Until those gaps are closed, comprehensive and accurate awareness should be reported as a quantified, provenance-preserving capability for a declared region, target population, sensor state, and prediction horizon—not as an unconditional claim of seeing everything.
